profiles.windows: Use an elevated Windows PowerShell 5.1 console on each sampled Windows device. Record OS build, collection time and device ID. Confirm the named built-in cmdlets exist with Get-Command. Do not change a policy to make a test succeed.
profiles.graph: Use PowerShell 7 and the Microsoft.Graph.Authentication module (Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Authentication -Scope CurrentUser, if your administrator permits it). Run Connect-MgGraph -TenantId <your-tenant-GUID> -Scopes <the delegated permissions below> -NoWelcome. Confirm Get-MgContext shows the intended tenant, account and scopes. A permitted reader role and admin consent may also be needed; consent is not a control change. Disconnect-MgGraph afterwards. The examples use the commercial-cloud v1.0 endpoint; choose the matching endpoint/profile for sovereign clouds.
profiles.exchange: Use PowerShell 7 and the ExchangeOnlineManagement module. Run Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName <your-auditor-UPN>. Use the least-privileged Exchange role that can read these settings (View-Only Configuration/View-Only Recipients as applicable). Defender for Office 365 cmdlets require the relevant service/licence and role. Confirm Get-ConnectionInformation reports the intended tenant; disconnect with Disconnect-ExchangeOnline.
profiles.purview: Use the ExchangeOnlineManagement module and Connect-IPPSSession -UserPrincipalName <your-auditor-UPN>. DLP readers need a role that exposes the DLP Get cmdlets; audit search uses Audit Reader/View-Only Audit Logs, and retention-policy access may need additional audit roles and licensing. Get-Command must find each required cmdlet before collecting. Keep exports in the approved assessment folder.
profiles.sharepoint: Use Windows PowerShell 5.1 with Microsoft.Online.SharePoint.PowerShell. Run Connect-SPOService -Url https://<tenant>-admin.sharepoint.com using an authorised SharePoint Administrator. SharePoint configuration reading commonly needs that role; do not claim a generic reader role is sufficient. Record the tenant and collection time.
profiles.teams: Use a supported PowerShell version and the MicrosoftTeams module. Run Connect-MicrosoftTeams -TenantId <tenant-GUID> with an authorised role able to read tenant and user policies. Resolve group-assigned and global policies as well as direct assignments.
profiles.azure: Use PowerShell 7 with Az.Accounts and the Az modules named by the commands. Run Connect-AzAccount -Tenant <tenant-GUID>, then Set-AzContext -Subscription <subscription-GUID>. Use Reader on the full assessment scope plus any named data-plane/backup roles. Repeat per subscription; a successful query in one subscription is not tenant coverage.
profiles.ad: Use Windows PowerShell 5.1 with the ActiveDirectory RSAT module from a domain-connected assessment host. Import-Module ActiveDirectory. Query the intended domain/DC with a permitted account. Run registry, SMB and service checks locally on every domain controller using an authorised elevated session. A standard domain read cannot prove protected ACL visibility or remote/DC coverage.
profiles.csv: Export the named records from the systems of record into an access-controlled assessment folder. Save UTF-8 CSV with the exact column names listed below, one row per scoped item. Record export time, scope, timezone and total population separately. These local PowerShell 5.1/7 checks inspect the supplied evidence only; the assessor must independently reconcile its completeness and validate its contents.
profiles.power: Use Windows PowerShell 5.1 with Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell and its documented dependencies. Run Add-PowerAppsAccount as a permitted Power Platform administrator. Confirm the tenant/environment inventory before exporting; Power Platform admin cmdlet support differs from PowerShell 7.
profiles.devops: Use PowerShell 7 or Windows PowerShell 5.1. Obtain a short-lived Azure DevOps PAT with Code (read) and Build (read) for the intended organisation/project, under its access policy. At Get-Credential enter any nonempty username and the PAT as password; do not paste a token into the script or transcript. This example reads policy/build metadata only. Revoke the test PAT afterwards.
profiles.dns: Run the DNS collection in Windows PowerShell 5.1 or a Windows PowerShell session with the DnsClient module. Reading DNS records does not require local administrator rights.

run_steps: Choose representative managed workstations and servers, including exception groups. In Intune open Endpoint security > App Control for Business and the policy device status; for Group Policy obtain the deployed policy and resultant GPO. Record target group, device, last sync, policy ID/version, rule collections and approved exceptions. A portal assignment or file on disk does not establish enforcement.

WDAC/App Control: run the WDAC branch on Windows 11 22H2 or later, or Server 2025 where CiTool is included. Match the organisation policy ID and base/supplemental IDs to the deployment record. IsEnforced means the policy is active; it alone does not prove deny enforcement. Inspect the matching source policy XML for option 3 (Enabled:Audit Mode), UMCI and script options, and corroborate the loaded policy with event 3099. Do not count only the built-in Microsoft driver blocklist as the organisation application policy. On earlier supported Windows, use deployed policy XML/version, the CodeIntegrity Operational log and the same behaviour tests; do not assume CiTool is present.

AppLocker: on a GPO/local-policy deployment run the AppLocker branch from the sampled endpoint, exporting effective XML. Inspect Exe, Dll, Msi, Script and Appx collections applicable to the scope; check enforced/audit-only modes, default/admin bypass rules, writable-path allow rules and AppIDSvc state. Test-AppLockerPolicy predicts the rule decision for the named user and file. It does not execute the file or establish runtime blocking.

AppLocker CSP/MDM deployment: Get-AppLockerPolicy only understands local/GPO policy and cannot retrieve CSP policy. Export the assigned ApplicationLaunchRestrictions policy XML and its device assignment/status from the MDM service, retain the policy identifier, and corroborate application with AppLocker device events and a runtime test. Do not label an empty GPO export as an absent CSP policy or as compliant.

Prepare two reviewed benign fixtures: one approved application and one unapproved application that performs no harmful action. Record their hashes and expected decisions. Confirm the negative fixture is not also trusted through a publisher rule, managed installer, reputation or supplemental policy; a renamed trusted executable is not necessarily unapproved. In a representative test environment sign in as the named standard user and launch each normally. Do not switch production enforcement off. Repeat for scripts, installers and a benign application loading a test DLL where those file types are in scope; use the relevant host and the same deployment path.

After the launches, rerun collection with a window covering the test. For WDAC match the negative fixture to CodeIntegrity event 3077 (blocked), not 3076 (audit/would block). For AppLocker match EXE/DLL events 8002 allowed, 8003 audit-only, 8004 blocked; MSI/Script events 8005/8006/8007 use the MSI and Script channel. WDAC script events in that channel use 8028 audit and 8029 enforcement; PowerShell may constrain a script rather than deny startup, so record language mode/actual restricted operation. Correlate file, hash when present, user, policy and timestamp with central logging.

Repeat the same approved and unapproved tests on each sampled policy/device/user combination. Record scope gaps and exemptions. Retain effective policy/MDM export, file hashes, static decisions, observed runtime outcome and matching local/central events.
TECH-APP-CONTROL.decision: Pass only for the sampled file types and users when the approved fixture works, an actually unauthorised benign fixture is denied or constrained as required, the intended policy is active in enforcement mode, and matching events reach the central collector. Audit-only, a policy ID alone, or static Allowed/Denied output is insufficient.
TECH-APP-CONTROL.limits: No application was launched or policy enforced by WACC. CiTool fields vary by OS. AppLocker CSP requires MDM evidence. Driver-only policy, DLL collection gaps, cached reputation and differing PowerShell hosts can change conclusions. Validate each applicable code type; an EXE test cannot prove script/DLL coverage.

run_steps: Export all policies, including disabled/report-only ones and exclusions. Identify the policies intended to protect each sampled role, application, device state and network location. Resolve nested/excluded group membership and authentication strengths.

In Entra Conditional Access > What If, evaluate a standard user, privileged user, excluded account, unmanaged device and legacy client against the selected resource. Save applied/not-applied policy reasons. What If predicts policy applicability; it does not issue a token or prove MFA happened.

With permitted test accounts perform one allowed and one expected-denied sign-in for each critical path. Revoke no production sessions for this test; use a fresh private browser or isolated test session and record UTC time/correlation ID.

Match the fresh sign-in in the returned audit records. Inspect conditionalAccessStatus, appliedConditionalAccessPolicies, authenticationDetails and status/error. Distinguish previously satisfied MFA/session claims from a newly performed factor.
TECH-CA.decision: Expected-denied cases must be denied by the intended enabled policy; allowed cases must satisfy the required strength/device conditions. Report-only policies do not pass enforcement.
TECH-CA.limits: Log retention, role, licence and API permissions can hide fields. Repeated successful MFA does not prove every excluded population is protected. A zero-row or redacted log is unknown.

TECH-MAIL-AUTH.command:
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
$domain = Read-Host 'An organisation-owned mail domain (no @)'
if ($domain -notmatch '^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$') { throw 'Enter a DNS domain.' }
Resolve-DnsName -Name $domain -Type TXT
Resolve-DnsName -Name ('_dmarc.'+$domain) -Type TXT
$dkim = Get-DkimSigningConfig -Identity $domain
$dkim | Select-Object Domain,Enabled,Status,Selector1CNAME,Selector2CNAME
Resolve-DnsName -Name ('selector1._domainkey.'+$domain) -Type CNAME
Resolve-DnsName -Name ('selector2._domainkey.'+$domain) -Type CNAME
run_steps: Inventory every sending domain and approved sender, including third-party services. Run DNS queries and compare answers from the organisation resolver and an approved independent resolver if DNS split views are possible.

Inspect one effective SPF record and authorised include chains, each published DKIM selector and active signing, and DMARC policy/report destinations. Resolve missing DNS responses; do not treat a lookup failure as enforcement.

Send a harmless uniquely tagged message through each approved sender to a controlled external mailbox. Inspect complete received headers: SPF/DKIM result, authentication alignment with From, and DMARC result.

In an agreed mail-testing environment exercise an unauthorised sender path using an organisation-controlled test domain/subdomain. Inspect quarantine/rejection, aggregate reports and recipient policy; do not spoof unrelated domains or send to real users.
TECH-MAIL-AUTH.decision: Approved senders authenticate and align; the unauthorised test path receives the intended DMARC action and is visible in reports.
TECH-MAIL-AUTH.limits: DNS configuration does not prove message delivery enforcement. Forwarding/ARC and recipient local policy affect results. DKIM selectors and policy choices must reflect the actual sending service.
